meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Owen's zero. Who decided it, and before or after anyone heard him?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.

Conclusive. Turnitin's own guide, printed in my bag, says that number should never be the sole basis for punishing a student, and your own procedure says the same. So I'll ask again: who decided, and was Owen heard first?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Now tell me what you actually have.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
11:31, 11:52, 11:58, I'm writing those down. He wrote it over the weekend, and pasting a finished draft from another file into a clean document looks exactly like that. What else do you have?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Show me the page. A seventeen-year-old misquoting Hamlet is sloppy, Hale, it isn't proof of anything. Is that line anywhere else in his work, or in the class notes?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Hand me the outline. Students change their minds between an outline and a final essay; that's the point of an outline. Where would a seventeen-year-old get "epistemological paralysis"?

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

Forty minutes in a classroom is not a weekend at home, and five minutes after class with no warning isn't a hearing. Whatever happens next, this stays off his record and it stays quiet, nothing in front of his class. Is anything on his record right now?

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

You still haven't told me whether anything is on his record right now, and I want that answer in the same email. Then Owen takes the rewrite, privately, to put this behind him, and the new mark is in well before his December 1 scholarship deadline. Give me a date for it.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Thursday, November 12, after school, then. Tonight's email has the rewrite, the date, the mark replacing the zero, and nothing on his record, in your words, with the principal copied.
Do we have an agreement?
Yes, once it's in my inbox tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

In today's meeting you agreed that Owen will complete a private, supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 on Thursday, November 12, after school, that its mark will replace the zero and be entered before December 1, and that nothing will be placed on his record. I still require written confirmation of each of those terms, along with a clear answer on whether anything is on Owen's record right now. I expect that email in my inbox tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: last position, agreeing to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, after school, and she still wants your written confirmation tonight and an answer on whether anything is on his record now; that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, reached before her time ran out.
What moved her: putting Owen's own dated work in front of her, the outline, your November 2 notes and his September in-class writing, because each was specific and something she could check herself.
What cost ground: opening with the 94 percent score and calling it conclusive, because to her a detector score is a machine's guess that its own maker says not to rely on alone.
What she never said: in October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history put the essay's creation at 11:31 PM on October 28, the night before it was due, which landed close to that kind of night; it proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: when she asked whether anything was on his record right now, answer it on the spot instead of moving to your offer, so it doesn't stay open into her email.
